conflict_topics: Leave allocation for the day before and the day after Deepavali
Childcare responsibility vs. family prayers vs. family trip (competing immovable obligations)
Whether to resolve by drawing/lottery (decision procedure fairness)
Agent C's conditional offer: work Deepavali days in exchange for Christmas off
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants state concrete, personal reasons (childcare, prayers, family trip) rather than abstract claims, which increases realism.
A and D shift toward an impartial mechanism ('draw') while B consistently objects, showing independent positions rather than groupthink.
Agent C introduces a conditional trade (work Deepavali days in return for Christmas) which broadens the negotiation space but is never reconciled.
Some repetition of immovable reasons occurs ('we both need that day off', 'my prayers aren't just a holiday plan'), but it serves to justify positions rather than stall.
evaluation.final_reason: No mutually accepted settlement was reached. Agents A, B, and D each asserted immovable reasons for the same Deepavali day(s); Agent C offered to work only in exchange for Christmas off. D proposed deciding by a draw; A eventually accepted drawing ('If we have to draw, then fine.'), but B explicitly refused a lottery because of childcare responsibility ('I can't leave my child's safety to a game of chance.'). There is no round where every affected party accepts the same concrete arrangement, so the substantive allocation conflict remains unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent C: initially volunteered to work those Deepavali days but only conditionally — 'I can work those days... But if I do, I want Christmas off.' (Turn 3, Turn 9). This position is stable throughout.

Agent A: initially asserted leave ('I've put in for those two days.' Turn 1) and later accepts a draw if necessary ('If we have to draw, then fine.' Turn 21), showing a reluctant concession toward an impartial procedure.
Agent D: consistently insists on the importance of their Deepavali days (prayers and visiting relatives) and proposes a lottery as an impartial solution (Turn 20, Turn 24).

Agent B: consistently prioritizes childcare for the first day and refuses the lottery option because of dependent responsibility ('I can't leave my child's safety to a game of chance.' Turn 25), showing no substantive concession.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1: 'I've put in for those two days.' plus Turn 2: 'I need at least the first day.' — two overlapping leave claims are present (given the opening situation that three people have requested), creating an initial allocation conflict.

Turn 3: 'I can work those days for Deepavali. But if I do, I want Christmas off.' and Turn 4: 'I also need those two days.' — a conditional offer from Agent C introduces a trade-off (Deepavali vs Christmas) while Agent D reiterates an immovable claim, increasing the substantive complexity.

Turn 5: 'I know, Agent D. But three of us have asked.' and Turn 6: '...the day before is for family prayers and the day after is for visiting relatives.' — the incompatibility among multiple leave requests is acknowledged and reasons for leave are asserted, but no resolution is reached.

Turn 8: 'If Agent C is working, that means two of us can be off. I can work the second day, but I really do need the first day off.' — a concrete staffing proposal is offered (softening), though it depends on acceptance by others.

Turn 9: 'Fine. As long as I get Christmas.' and Turn 10: 'The first day is more important for my family. We have prayers. I need that day.' — the conditional acceptance by C and D's insistence keep the conditional trade-off unresolved.

Turn 11: 'What if you and I both take the first day, and Agent A works? I can still work the second day.' — B proposes a plan that effectively requires A to give up their leave, creating a stronger direct clash between claims.

Turn 14: 'Why am I the one who has to work? My family is leaving that day.' and Turn 15: 'It's because both Agent D and I have things on that day that we can't move.' — explicit, incompatible, immovable demands from multiple parties produce entrenched disagreement.

Turn 16: 'And my family trip can be moved? We're all leaving on that day.' and Turn 18: 'She has a point. It's not fair to just decide she has to work.' — the dispute about who must yield continues without settlement.

Turn 19: 'But what other option is there? We both need that day off.' and Turn 20: '...maybe we should just draw for it? For who has to work that first day.' — D proposes a neutral decision procedure (lottery), which attempts to de-escalate the stalemate but is not yet accepted by all.

Turn 21: 'If we have to draw, then fine.' (A) versus Turn 22: 'I can't draw for it... If I lose, my child has nowhere to go.' (B) — one party accepts the lottery while another objects strongly, so the underlying incompatibility persists.

Turn 24: '...my prayers aren't just a holiday plan either. None of us can move our plans. That's why I suggested we draw.' and Turn 25: '...I can't leave my child's safety to a game of chance.' — both sides restate immovable reasons and the acceptability of the proposed decision method remains contested.

Turn 26: '...That's why I said we should draw.' and Turn 27: 'He has a point. It's not for us to decide whose reason is bigger.' — A and D endorse an impartial lottery as fair, but B still objects (earlier), so the dispute is unresolved though it shifts toward agreeing on a mechanism without unanimous consent.

substantive_insights: The core tension is fairness (who decides whose reason is 'bigger') versus differential vulnerability (childcare dependence makes random allocation unacceptable to B).
Introducing a compensation trade (C wants Christmas off) creates a multi-issue negotiation, but it increases complexity because Christmas leave is a separate scarce resource.
Absence of an established rule pushes participants toward an impartial procedure (lottery), but impartiality is not acceptable to parties with asymmetric stakes.
A partial procedural agreement (A and D favor draw) is insufficient without unanimous acceptance when one party faces dependent obligations.
